notes.h: Who makes and runs the rules
notes.b: Anti-doping (the effort to stop athletes using banned drugs and methods) works on two levels. An international agency writes the rules, and a national body applies them in each country.
points: The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) sets the World Anti-Doping Code, the single set of rules for the world, and the Prohibited List, the list of substances and methods that athletes are banned from using.
In Ireland, Sport Ireland (the national sports body) runs the Irish Anti-Doping Programme and the Irish Anti-Doping Rules, so the world rules are put into practice at home.

The Irish rules apply the World Anti-Doping Code to all athletes in sports governed by national governing bodies (NGBs, such as the association that runs a sport in Ireland) that Sport Ireland recognises.
notes.tip: Keep to the current Irish rules. Do not describe historical rules or older sanction lengths.

notes.b: The rules do not ask what the athlete meant to do. They look only at what is found in the athlete's body, and this principle is called strict liability.
points: Athletes are responsible for any prohibited substance found in their body, whether or not they intended to cheat, so claiming it was an accident is not a defence.
Athletes must therefore check every medicine and supplement (such as a vitamin or protein product) they take before taking it, because anything they swallow could contain a banned substance.
notes.tip: Prescribed medicine is not automatically allowed, so remember that a check is needed before taking anything.

notes.b: An anti-doping rule violation is any act that breaks the anti-doping rules. The list goes well beyond failing a test, and it also covers people around the athlete.
points: Presence: a prohibited substance, its metabolites (the substances the body breaks it down into) or markers (signs that it was used) found in a sample taken from the athlete.
Use: use or attempted use of a prohibited substance or method, so an athlete can be in breach even if the attempt did not work.
Refusal: evading, refusing or failing to submit to sample collection after being notified, so an athlete cannot avoid a test without consequences.

Whereabouts failures: three missed tests and/or filing failures (not giving required location details on time) within 12 months. Whereabouts means the athlete's location, given in advance for testing.
Tampering: tampering or attempted tampering with any part of doping control (the testing process), such as interfering with a sample.
Possession: possession of a prohibited substance or method.
Trafficking: trafficking or attempted trafficking, including selling a prohibited substance, so selling a performance-enhancing drug (PED) is itself a violation.
Administration: administering or attempting to administer a prohibited substance or method to an athlete, which can involve coaches or doctors rather than the athlete.
Complicity: assisting or covering up a violation. Prohibited association: working with a banned coach or doctor.
notes.tip: Selling a PED is a violation (trafficking), and athletes cannot refuse a test without consequences. If asked for two rules an athlete may have broken when the substance is unknown, refusing a test and whereabouts failures are accepted examples. Exams ask you to state two or four current Irish anti-doping rules.

notes.h: Testing, whereabouts and the athlete biological passport
notes.b: Rules only work if they are enforced. Samples, advance location details and long-term monitoring are three ways Ireland checks that athletes follow them.
points: Testing: urine and blood samples are taken in competition and out of competition, often with no advance notice, so athletes cannot time their drug use around a known test.
Each sample is sealed and split into an A and a B sample, which are analysed in WADA-accredited laboratories (labs approved by WADA).
The B sample can be tested to confirm a positive A sample, which gives the athlete a second check on the result.
Whereabouts: athletes in the registered testing pool (the group of athletes chosen for testing) give their location in advance, so testers know where to find them.
The whereabouts requirement includes a daily 60-minute slot when the athlete is available for testing.
Athlete biological passport: blood and steroid markers are monitored over time to detect the effects of doping, so doping can be spotted from changes even when no banned substance is found.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to identify three ways the rules are enforced. Testing, whereabouts and the athlete biological passport are three.

notes.b: Once a possible violation is found, a fixed process decides whether the athlete is guilty and what the penalty is. Each step is designed to be fair to the athlete.
points: Sport Ireland notifies the athlete of the suspected violation.
An independent disciplinary panel (a group not linked to Sport Ireland) hears the case, and appeals are possible, so a decision can be challenged.
Sanctions (penalties) include disqualification of results and loss of medals and prize money.
Sanctions include a period of ineligibility (a time when the athlete is banned from competing), normally four years for an intentional first violation.
The decision is published.
notes.tip: Give four years only for an intentional first violation, and do not give other sanction lengths.

notes.b: Enforcement is not only testing. Ireland also tries to prevent doping through teaching and to catch it by other means.
points: Anti-doping education programmes are run for athletes and support staff (coaches, doctors and others who work with athletes), so that they know the rules and the risks.
Investigations use information from sources other than sample tests, so doping can be uncovered even when an athlete has never failed a test.

notes.b: Some athletes have genuine medical conditions that need drugs which are on the Prohibited List. A therapeutic use exemption lets them take the medicine legally, provided strict conditions are met.
points: A therapeutic use exemption (TUE) is permission to use a prohibited substance or method to treat a diagnosed medical condition. It is the circumstance in which an athlete can compete with a banned substance in their system.
The athlete applies in advance, except in an emergency, to the relevant anti-doping organisation, with medical evidence.
An independent panel of doctors decides the application.
Condition 1: the athlete's health would be significantly impaired without the substance or method.
Condition 2: it gives no additional performance enhancement beyond a return to normal health, so the athlete is treated but not given an advantage.
Condition 3: there is no reasonable permitted alternative. Condition 4: the need is not a consequence of earlier use without a TUE.
Examples: insulin for type 1 diabetes; certain asthma medications taken above the permitted doses; prescribed stimulant medication for diagnosed ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder).
A doctor's prescription alone does not make a prohibited medicine allowed; a TUE is needed, because a doctor's prescription does not by itself give permission under the anti-doping rules.
notes.tip: Exams ask what a TUE is, when TUEs are used, and for two circumstances where Sport Ireland might grant one. The three examples above cover this. Prescribed medicine is not automatically allowed.

notes.h: What a violation means for the performer and the activity
notes.b: Doping harms more than the athlete who is caught. The consequences fall on the performer and on the activity (the sport) as a whole.
points: For the performer: a ban, disqualification of results, loss of medals, funding and sponsorship, damage to reputation, and the health risks of the drug itself.
For the activity: lost credibility and public trust, withdrawal of sponsors and broadcasters, and young people and parents turning away from the sport, which means fewer people take part.
notes.tip: There is more on this in Drugs and sport, where the categories of PED and their effects are covered.

keyTerms.definition: A breach of the anti-doping rules, such as a positive test, a refused test or a whereabouts failure.
The principle that an athlete is responsible for any prohibited substance found in their body, whether or not they intended to cheat.
Permission, granted under strict conditions, to use a prohibited substance or method to treat a diagnosed medical condition.
The information an athlete in the registered testing pool gives in advance about where they can be found for testing.
The group of athletes who must provide whereabouts information so that they can be tested out of competition.
A record of an athlete's blood and steroid markers over time, used to detect the effects of doping.
The two parts of a sample, each analysed in a WADA-accredited laboratory, so that a result can be confirmed.
A period during which an athlete is banned from competing.
A panel that hears an anti-doping case independently and decides on sanctions.
The body that runs the Irish Anti-Doping Programme and the Irish Anti-Doping Rules.
Selling, supplying or distributing a prohibited substance or method, or attempting to do so.

factCards.term: Whereabouts failures that count as a violation
factCards.definition: Three missed tests and/or filing failures within 12 months.

factCards.term: The four conditions for a TUE
factCards.definition: Health significantly impaired without it; no additional performance enhancement beyond a return to normal health; no reasonable permitted alternative; the need is not caused by earlier use without a TUE.
Insulin for type 1 diabetes, and prescribed stimulant medication for diagnosed ADHD.

factCards.term: Five ways Irish anti-doping rules are enforced
factCards.definition: Testing in and out of competition; whereabouts requirements; the athlete biological passport; results management, hearings and sanctions; education and investigation.

questions.prompt: State four current Irish anti-doping rules.
questions.model: 1. The presence of a prohibited substance, its metabolites or markers in a sample. 2. The use or attempted use of a prohibited substance or method. 3. Evading, refusing or failing to submit to sample collection after being notified. 4. Whereabouts failures: three missed tests and/or filing failures within 12 months.

questions.prompt: Explain therapeutic use exemption and describe two circumstances in which one might be granted.
questions.model: A therapeutic use exemption (TUE) is permission to use a prohibited substance or method to treat a diagnosed medical condition. The athlete applies in advance, with medical evidence, to the relevant anti-doping organisation, and an independent panel of doctors decides. It is granted only if the athlete's health would be significantly impaired without the medicine, if it gives no performance benefit beyond a return to normal health, and if there is no reasonable permitted alternative. Circumstance 1: an athlete with type 1 diabetes who needs insulin. Circumstance 2: an athlete with diagnosed ADHD who takes prescribed stimulant medication.

questions.prompt: Identify three ways in which Irish anti-doping rules are enforced.
questions.model: 1. Testing: urine and blood samples are taken in and out of competition, often without notice, and analysed in WADA-accredited laboratories. 2. Whereabouts: athletes in the registered testing pool give their location in advance, including a daily 60-minute slot for testing. 3. Sanctions after a hearing: an independent panel can disqualify results, remove medals and prize money, and impose a ban, normally four years for an intentional first violation.
